## 31.7.9. Vector Load/Store Whole Register Instructions

Format for Vector Load Whole Register Instructions under LOAD-FP major opcode

<image>

Format for Vector Store Whole Register Instructions under STORE-FP major opcode

<image>

These instructions load and store whole vector register groups.

<image>

These instructions are intended to be used to save and restore vector registers when the type or length of the current contents of the vector register is not known, or where modifying vl and vtype would be costly. Examples include compiler register spills, vector function calls where values are passed in vector registers, interrupt handlers, and OS context switches. Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the vlenb register.

The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit-stride loads.

<image>

Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. NFIELDS indicates the number of vector registers to transfer, numbered successively after the base. Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2,  4,  8  are  supported,  with  other  values  reserved.  When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart

```
≥ evl .
```

The  instructions  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  unit-stride  load  and  store  instructions,  with  the  base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1 .

Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8).

<image>

Allowing  misaligned  exceptions  to  be  raised  based  on  non-alignment  to  the  encoded  EEW simplifies the implementation of these instructions. Some subset implementations might not support smaller SEW widths, so are allowed to report misaligned exceptions for the smallest supported SEW even if larger than encoded EEW. An extreme non-standard implementation might  have  SEWMIN >XLEN for  example.  Software  environments  can  mandate  the  minimum alignment requirements to support an ABI.

```
# Format of whole register load and store instructions. vl1r.v v3, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl1re8.v vl1re8.v    v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/8 bytes held at address in a0 vl1re16.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl1re32.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl1re64.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl2r.v v2, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl2re8.v vl2re8.v    v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl2re16.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl2re32.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl2re64.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl4r.v v4, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl4re8.v vl4re8.v    v4, (a0)  # Load v4-v7 with 4*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl4re16.v   v4, (a0) vl4re32.v   v4, (a0) vl4re64.v   v4, (a0) vl8r.v v8, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl8re8.v vl8re8.v    v8, (a0)  # Load v8-v15 with 8*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl8re16.v   v8, (a0) vl8re32.v   v8, (a0) vl8re64.v   v8, (a0) vs1r.v v3, (a1)      # Store v3 to address in a1 vs2r.v v2, (a1)      # Store v2-v3 to address in a1 vs4r.v v4, (a1)      # Store v4-v7 to address in a1
```

RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Instruction syntax (pseudoinstruction)**  
  ```
  vl1re32.v   v3, (a0)   # Load v3 with VLEN/32 words held at address in a0
  ```

- **Encoding and EEW**  
  The load instruction has an EEW encoded in the *mew* and *width* fields "following the pattern of regular unit‑stride loads". For **vl1re32.v**, the encoded EEW is 32.

- **Number of registers transferred (NFIELDS)**  
  The *nf* field encodes how many vector registers to load. For **vl1re32.v** the encoded number of registers is 1 (NFIELDS = 1), which "must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved". Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2, 4, 8 are supported.

- **Effective vector length (evl)**  
  The instructions operate with an effective vector length  
  ```
  evl = NFIELDS * VLEN / EEW
  ```  
  For **vl1re32.v**, *evl* = 1 × VLEN / 32 = VLEN/32, "regardless of current settings in vtype and vl".

- **Reservation condition**  
  The usual property that no elements are written if *vstart* ≥ *vl* "does not apply to these instructions". Instead, "the instructions are reserved if vstart ≥ evl". Therefore **vl1re32.v** is reserved when *vstart* ≥ VLEN/32.

- **Memory layout**  
  "Because in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW." Thus **vl1re32.v** writes the raw byte contents from memory into the destination register.

- **Base address register**  
  The instructions operate similarly to unmasked unit‑stride load instructions, "with the base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1".

- **Misaligned address exception**  
  Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole‑register loads "if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8)." For **vl1re32.v**, this means an exception may be raised if the address is not naturally aligned to max(32/8 = 4 bytes, SEWMIN/8).

- **Behavior relative to *vtype* and *vl***  
  The instruction "operates with an effective vector length … regardless of current settings in vtype and vl". Consequently, **vl1re32.v** does not depend on the current *vtype* or *vl* settings for its operation.

<image>

These instructions load and store whole vector register groups.

<image>

These instructions are intended to be used to save and restore vector registers when the type or length of the current contents of the vector register is not known, or where modifying vl and vtype would be costly. Examples include compiler register spills, vector function calls where values are passed in vector registers, interrupt handlers, and OS context switches. Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the vlenb register.

The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit-stride loads.

<image>

Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. NFIELDS indicates the number of vector registers to transfer, numbered successively after the base. Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2,  4,  8  are  supported,  with  other  values  reserved.  When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart

```
≥ evl .
```

The  instructions  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  unit-stride  load  and  store  instructions,  with  the  base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1 .

Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8).

<image>

Allowing  misaligned  exceptions  to  be  raised  based  on  non-alignment  to  the  encoded  EEW simplifies the implementation of these instructions. Some subset implementations might not support smaller SEW widths, so are allowed to report misaligned exceptions for the smallest supported SEW even if larger than encoded EEW. An extreme non-standard implementation might  have  SEWMIN >XLEN for  example.  Software  environments  can  mandate  the  minimum alignment requirements to support an ABI.

```
# Format of whole register load and store instructions. vl1r.v v3, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl1re8.v vl1re8.v    v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/8 bytes held at address in a0 vl1re16.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl1re32.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl1re64.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl2r.v v2, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl2re8.v vl2re8.v    v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl2re16.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl2re32.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl2re64.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl4r.v v4, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl4re8.v vl4re8.v    v4, (a0)  # Load v4-v7 with 4*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl4re16.v   v4, (a0) vl4re32.v   v4, (a0) vl4re64.v   v4, (a0) vl8r.v v8, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl8re8.v vl8re8.v    v8, (a0)  # Load v8-v15 with 8*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl8re16.v   v8, (a0) vl8re32.v   v8, (a0) vl8re64.v   v8, (a0) vs1r.v v3, (a1)      # Store v3 to address in a1 vs2r.v v2, (a1)      # Store v2-v3 to address in a1 vs4r.v v4, (a1)      # Store v4-v7 to address in a1
```

## vs8r.v v8, (a1)      # Store v8-v15 to address in a1

<image>

We have considered adding a whole register mask load instruction ( vl1rm.v ) but have decided to omit from initial extension. The primary purpose would be to inform the microarchitecture that the data will be used as a mask. The same effect can be achieved with the following code sequence, whose cost is at most four instructions. Of these, the first could likely be removed as vl is often already in a scalar register, and the last might already be present if the following vector instruction needs a new SEW/LMUL. So, in best case only two instructions (of which only  one  performs  vector  operations)  are  needed  to  synthesize  the  effect  of  the  dedicated instruction:

```
csrr t0, vl                        # Save current vl (potentially not needed) vsetvli t1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma     # Maximum VLMAX vlm.v v0, (a0)                     # Load mask register vsetvli x0, t0, <new type>         # Restore vl (potentially already present)
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Mnemonic and Pseudoinstruction Mapping**  
  `vl2re8.v v2, (a0)` is a pseudoinstruction equal to `vl2re8.v    v2, (a0)` and loads vector registers v2‑v3 with 2 × VLEN/8 bytes from the address in a0.

- **Encoding Fields**  
  * The instruction is a whole‑register load; the EEW is encoded as 8 bits in the *mew* and *width* fields following the pattern of regular unit‑stride loads.  
  * The *nf* field encodes the number of vector registers to transfer. For `vl2re8.v`, *nf* = 2, which is a supported NFIELDS value (only 1, 2, 4, 8 are supported). The encoded number of registers **must be a power of 2** and the vector register numbers **must be aligned** as with a vector register group; otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved.

- **Memory Layout**  
  When multiple registers are transferred, the lowest‑numbered vector register is held in the lowest‑numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory. Thus `vl2re8.v` loads v2 from the base address and v3 from the address offset by VLEN/8 bytes.

- **Effective Vector Length (evl)**  
  The instruction operates with an effective vector length  
  `evl = NFIELDS × VLEN / EEW`.  
  For `vl2re8.v`, `evl = 2 × VLEN / 8`.  
  The usual property that no elements are written if `vstart ≥ vl` does **not** apply. The instruction is **reserved if `vstart ≥ evl`**.

- **Base Address**  
  The base address is passed in the scalar integer register specified by `rs1`, the same as for unmasked unit‑stride load instructions.

- **Misaligned Address Exception**  
  Implementations **are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception** on whole‑register loads if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of:
  * the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8`), and
  * the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  
  For `vl2re8.v`, `EEW/8 = 1` byte, so the alignment requirement is at least `SEWMIN/8` bytes.

- **Byte Transfer Count**  
  Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the `vlenb` register; for `vl2re8.v` the transfer size is `2 × VLEN/8` bytes.

=========
============================================================
**VL2RE16.V (vector‑load‑whole‑register, 2 registers, EEW = 16)**  

- **Operation** – Loads two consecutive vector registers (the base register and the next higher‑numbered register) from memory starting at the address in the scalar x register specified by rs1.  
  - Pseudocode from the text:  
    `vl2re16.v   v2, (a0)   # Load v2‑v3 with 2*VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0`

- **Encoding fields** – The nf field encodes the number of registers to transfer (NFIELDS = 2). The EEW is encoded in the mew and width fields as 16 bits.

- **Effective vector length** – The instruction operates with an effective vector length  
  `evl = NFIELDS * VLEN / EEW`  
  For VL2RE16.V this is `evl = 2 * VLEN / 16`.  
  This length is used **regardless of current settings in vtype and vl**.

- **Reservation condition** – The usual property that "no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl" **does not apply**.  
  Instead, the instruction **is reserved if vstart ≥ evl**.

- **Alignment and exception handling** – Implementations are **allowed to raise a misaligned address exception** on whole‑register loads (including VL2RE16.V) if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of:  
  1. the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8`), or  
  2. the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  

- **Register‑group alignment** – The encoded number of registers **must be a power of 2** and the vector register numbers **must be aligned as with a vector register group**, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved.  
  Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2, 4, 8 are supported; other values are reserved.

- **Memory layout** – Because **in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts**, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. The lowest‑numbered vector register receives the data at the lowest‑numbered memory addresses; successive registers are placed contiguously in memory.

- **Behavior compared with other whole‑register loads** – VL2RE16.V **operates similarly to unmasked unit‑stride load instructions**, with the base address passed in the scalar x register (rs1). All shared properties (effective‑vector‑length computation, reservation rule, alignment exception policy, register‑group alignment requirement) apply to VL2RE16.V in the same way as to other whole‑register load instructions (e.g., VL1RE8.V, VL4RE32.V, etc.).

  Implementations **are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception** on this whole‑register load if the base address **is not naturally aligned to the larger of**  
  * the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8`), **or**  
  * the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  

- **Byte count transferred**  
  Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the `vlenb` register; for `vl2re32.v` the transfer size is `2 * VLEN / 8` bytes (i.e., `2 * VLEN/32` words).  

- **Pseudocode example (from the specification)**  

  ```
  vl2re32.v   v2, (a0)   # Load v2‑v3 with 2*VLEN/32 words held at address in a0
  ```

## 31.7.9. Vector Load/Store Whole Register Instructions

Format for Vector Load Whole Register Instructions under LOAD-FP major opcode

<image>

Format for Vector Store Whole Register Instructions under STORE-FP major opcode

<image>

These instructions load and store whole vector register groups.

<image>

These instructions are intended to be used to save and restore vector registers when the type or length of the current contents of the vector register is not known, or where modifying vl and vtype would be costly. Examples include compiler register spills, vector function calls where values are passed in vector registers, interrupt handlers, and OS context switches. Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the vlenb register.

The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit-stride loads.

<image>

Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. NFIELDS indicates the number of vector registers to transfer, numbered successively after the base. Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2,  4,  8  are  supported,  with  other  values  reserved.  When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart

```
≥ evl .
```

The  instructions  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  unit-stride  load  and  store  instructions,  with  the  base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1 .

Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8).

<image>

Allowing  misaligned  exceptions  to  be  raised  based  on  non-alignment  to  the  encoded  EEW simplifies the implementation of these instructions. Some subset implementations might not support smaller SEW widths, so are allowed to report misaligned exceptions for the smallest supported SEW even if larger than encoded EEW. An extreme non-standard implementation might  have  SEWMIN >XLEN for  example.  Software  environments  can  mandate  the  minimum alignment requirements to support an ABI.

```
# Format of whole register load and store instructions. vl1r.v v3, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl1re8.v vl1re8.v    v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/8 bytes held at address in a0 vl1re16.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl1re32.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl1re64.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl2r.v v2, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl2re8.v vl2re8.v    v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl2re16.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl2re32.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl2re64.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl4r.v v4, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl4re8.v vl4re8.v    v4, (a0)  # Load v4-v7 with 4*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl4re16.v   v4, (a0) vl4re32.v   v4, (a0) vl4re64.v   v4, (a0) vl8r.v v8, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl8re8.v vl8re8.v    v8, (a0)  # Load v8-v15 with 8*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl8re16.v   v8, (a0) vl8re32.v   v8, (a0) vl8re64.v   v8, (a0) vs1r.v v3, (a1)      # Store v3 to address in a1 vs2r.v v2, (a1)      # Store v2-v3 to address in a1 vs4r.v v4, (a1)      # Store v4-v7 to address in a1
```

## vs8r.v v8, (a1)      # Store v8-v15 to address in a1

<image>

We have considered adding a whole register mask load instruction ( vl1rm.v ) but have decided to omit from initial extension. The primary purpose would be to inform the microarchitecture that the data will be used as a mask. The same effect can be achieved with the following code sequence, whose cost is at most four instructions. Of these, the first could likely be removed as vl is often already in a scalar register, and the last might already be present if the following vector instruction needs a new SEW/LMUL. So, in best case only two instructions (of which only  one  performs  vector  operations)  are  needed  to  synthesize  the  effect  of  the  dedicated instruction:

```
csrr t0, vl                        # Save current vl (potentially not needed) vsetvli t1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma     # Maximum VLMAX vlm.v v0, (a0)                     # Load mask register vsetvli x0, t0, <new type>         # Restore vl (potentially already present)
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Instruction form**: `vl2re64.v   v2, (a0)` is a pseudoinstruction that loads vector registers `v2‑v3` with `2*VLEN/64` doublewords held at the address in `a0`.  

- **Encoding fields**  
  - The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the *mew* and *width* fields following the pattern of regular unit‑stride loads.  
  - The *nf* field encodes how many vector registers to load and store using the NFIELDS encoding (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. **Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2, 4, 8 are supported**, with other values reserved.  

- **Effective vector length**  
  - The instructions operate with an effective vector length, `evl = NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW`, regardless of current settings in *vtype* and *vl*.  
  - The usual property that no elements are written if `vstart ≥ vl` does **not** apply to these instructions.  
  - Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if `vstart` exceeds the largest element index for the current *vtype* setting does **not** apply.  
  - Instead, the instructions are reserved if `vstart ≥ evl`.  

- **Memory ordering and address handling**  
  - The instructions operate similarly to unmasked unit‑stride load and store instructions, with the base address passed in the scalar *x* register specified by *rs1*.  
  - Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8`) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  

- **Transfer layout**  
  - When multiple registers are transferred, the lowest‑numbered vector register is held in the lowest‑numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.  

- **Software visibility**  
  - Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the *vlenb* register.  

- **Byte‑layout equivalence**  
  - Because in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence it would have sufficed to provide only EEW = 8 variants; the full set of EEW variants is provided so that the encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

## vs8r.v v8, (a1)      # Store v8-v15 to address in a1

<image>

We have considered adding a whole register mask load instruction ( vl1rm.v ) but have decided to omit from initial extension. The primary purpose would be to inform the microarchitecture that the data will be used as a mask. The same effect can be achieved with the following code sequence, whose cost is at most four instructions. Of these, the first could likely be removed as vl is often already in a scalar register, and the last might already be present if the following vector instruction needs a new SEW/LMUL. ```

============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Instruction form**: `vl4re8.v  v4, (a0)`  
  - Pseudoinstruction `vl4r.v v4, (a0)` is defined as equal to `vl4re8.v v4, (a0)`.  
  - Loads vector registers **v4‑v7** (four registers) from memory starting at the address in scalar register `a0`.

- **Encoding fields**  
  - The `nf` field encodes the number of registers transferred. For `vl4re8.v` the encoded `NFIELDS` value is **4**.  
  - `NFIELDS` **must be a power of 2** and **must be one of 1, 2, 4, 8**; other values are reserved.  
  - The `mew` and `width` fields encode an **EEW of 8 bits** (EEW = 8) following the pattern of regular unit‑stride loads.

- **Effective vector length**  
  - The instruction operates with an **effective vector length** `evl = NFIELDS * VLEN / EEW`.  
  - For `vl4re8.v`: `evl = 4 * VLEN / 8`.  
  - The instruction **ignores the current `vtype` and `vl` settings**; they do not affect its operation.

- **Reservation condition**  
  - The instruction is **reserved** if `vstart ≥ evl`.  
  - The usual property that no elements are written when `vstart ≥ vl` **does not apply** to this instruction.

- **Memory layout**  
  - When multiple registers are transferred, **the lowest‑numbered vector register is placed at the lowest‑numbered memory address**, and successive vector registers are stored contiguously in memory.  
  - Thus, memory at the base address holds the contents of `v4`, followed immediately by `v5`, `v6`, and `v7`.

- **Address alignment and exceptions**  
  - The **base address** is taken from the scalar integer register specified by `rs1` (e.g., `a0`).  
  - Implementations **are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception** if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of:
    - the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8` = 1 byte for EEW = 8), and  
    - the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  

- **Data layout equivalence**  
  - Because **in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts**, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of the EEW value.  

- **Operational similarity**  
  - `vl4re8.v` **operates similarly to an unmasked unit‑stride load** instruction, with the only difference being the whole‑register transfer of four registers.

## vs8r.v v8, (a1)      # Store v8-v15 to address in a1

<image>

We have considered adding a whole register mask load instruction ( vl1rm.v ) but have decided to omit from initial extension. The primary purpose would be to inform the microarchitecture that the data will be used as a mask. The same effect can be achieved with the following code sequence, whose cost is at most four instructions. Of these, the first could likely be removed as vl is often already in a scalar register, and the last might already be present if the following vector instruction needs a new SEW/LMUL. So, in best case only two instructions (of which only  one  performs  vector  operations)  are  needed  to  synthesize  the  effect  of  the  dedicated instruction:

```
csrr t0, vl                        # Save current vl (potentially not needed) vsetvli t1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma     # Maximum VLMAX vlm.v v0, (a0)                     # Load mask register vsetvli x0, t0, <new type>         # Restore vl (potentially already present)
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
These are whole‑register load instructions that load a group of four consecutive vector registers (the destination register group is numbered successively after the base register). The instruction is encoded with EEW = 16 (the "re16" suffix) and NFIELDS = 4.

- "These instructions load and store whole vector register groups."  
- "The nf field encodes how many vector registers to load and store using the NFIELDS encoding (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved."  
- "Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2, 4, 8 are supported, with other values reserved."  
- "When multiple registers are transferred, the lowest‑numbered vector register is held in the lowest‑numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory."  

Effective‑vector‑length behavior:

- "The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl = NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl."  
- "The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions."  
- "Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply."  
- "Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart ≥ evl."  

Addressing and alignment:

- "The instructions operate similarly to unmasked unit‑stride load and store instructions, with the base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1."  
- "Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8)."

Data‑layout hint:

- "Because in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide only EEW=8 variants. The full set of EEW variants is provided so that the encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally."

## 31.7.9. Vector Load/Store Whole Register Instructions

Format for Vector Load Whole Register Instructions under LOAD-FP major opcode

<image>

Format for Vector Store Whole Register Instructions under STORE-FP major opcode

<image>

These instructions load and store whole vector register groups.

<image>

These instructions are intended to be used to save and restore vector registers when the type or length of the current contents of the vector register is not known, or where modifying vl and vtype would be costly. Examples include compiler register spills, vector function calls where values are passed in vector registers, interrupt handlers, and OS context switches. Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the vlenb register.

The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit-stride loads.

<image>

Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. NFIELDS indicates the number of vector registers to transfer, numbered successively after the base. Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2,  4,  8  are  supported,  with  other  values  reserved.  When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart

```
≥ evl .
```

The  instructions  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  unit-stride  load  and  store  instructions,  with  the  base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1 .

Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8).

<image>

Allowing  misaligned  exceptions  to  be  raised  based  on  non-alignment  to  the  encoded  EEW simplifies the implementation of these instructions. Some subset implementations might not support smaller SEW widths, so are allowed to report misaligned exceptions for the smallest supported SEW even if larger than encoded EEW. An extreme non-standard implementation might  have  SEWMIN >XLEN for  example.  Software  environments  can  mandate  the  minimum alignment requirements to support an ABI.


Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. NFIELDS indicates the number of vector registers to transfer, numbered successively after the base. Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2,  4,  8  are  supported,  with  other  values  reserved.  When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart

```
≥ evl .
```

The  instructions  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  unit-stride  load  and  store  instructions,  with  the  base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1 .

Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8).

<image>

Allowing  misaligned  exceptions  to  be  raised  based  on  non-alignment  to  the  encoded  EEW simplifies the implementation of these instructions. Some subset implementations might not support smaller SEW widths, so are allowed to report misaligned exceptions for the smallest supported SEW even if larger than encoded EEW. An extreme non-standard implementation might  have  SEWMIN >XLEN for  example.  Software  environments  can  mandate  the  minimum alignment requirements to support an ABI.

```
# Format of whole register load and store instructions. vl1r.v v3, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl1re8.v vl1re8.v    v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/8 bytes held at address in a0 vl1re16.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl1re32.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl1re64.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl2r.v v2, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl2re8.v vl2re8.v    v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl2re16.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl2re32.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl2re64.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl4r.v v4, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl4re8.v vl4re8.v    v4, (a0)  # Load v4-v7 with 4*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl4re16.v   v4, (a0) vl4re32.v   v4, (a0) vl4re64.v   v4, (a0) vl8r.v v8, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl8re8.v vl8re8.v    v8, (a0)  # Load v8-v15 with 8*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl8re16.v   v8, (a0) vl8re32.v   v8, (a0) vl8re64.v   v8, (a0) vs1r.v v3, (a1)      # Store v3 to address in a1 vs2r.v v2, (a1)      # Store v2-v3 to address in a1 vs4r.v v4, (a1)      # Store v4-v7 to address in a1
```

## vs8r.v v8, (a1)      # Store v8-v15 to address in a1

<image>

We have considered adding a whole register mask load instruction ( vl1rm.v ) but have decided to omit from initial extension. The primary purpose would be to inform the microarchitecture that the data will be used as a mask. The same effect can be achieved with the following code sequence, whose cost is at most four instructions. Of these, the first could likely be removed as vl is often already in a scalar register, and the last might already be present if the following vector instruction needs a new SEW/LMUL. So, in best case only two instructions (of which only  one  performs  vector  operations)  are  needed  to  synthesize  the  effect  of  the  dedicated instruction:

```
csrr t0, vl                        # Save current vl (potentially not needed) vsetvli t1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma     # Maximum VLMAX vlm.v v0, (a0)                     # Load mask register vsetvli x0, t0, <new type>         # Restore vl (potentially already present)
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Mnemonic and Encoding**  
  - The instruction is encoded as **vl8re8.v** (pseudo‑instruction **vl8r.v**).  
  - The **nf** field is set to **8**, which is one of the only supported NFIELDS values (1, 2, 4, 8). The encoded number of registers **must** be a power of two and the vector register numbers **must** be aligned as with a vector register group; otherwise the encoding is reserved.  

- **Operation and Effective Vector Length**  
  - The instruction loads **8 consecutive vector registers** (v8 – v15) from memory, with the lowest‑numbered register placed at the lowest‑addressed memory location and successive registers stored contiguously.  
  - It operates with an **effective vector length** `evl = NFIELDS * VLEN / EEW`. For this instruction `NFIELDS = 8` and `EEW = 8`, so `evl = 8 * VLEN / 8 = VLEN`.  
  - The instruction **ignores the current settings of `vtype` and `vl`**; it always uses the effective vector length described above.  

- **vstart Handling**  
  - The usual property that no elements are written if `vstart ≥ vl` **does not apply** to this instruction.  
  - The instruction is **reserved** if `vstart ≥ evl` (i.e., if `vstart ≥ VLEN`).  

- **Addressing**  
  - The base address is supplied in the scalar integer register `rs1`.  
  - The instruction **operates similarly to an unmasked unit‑stride load**; no mask is applied.  

- **Alignment and Exceptions**  
  - Implementations are **allowed to raise a misaligned address exception** on whole‑register loads if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of:  
    1. the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8`), or  
    2. the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  
  - For `vl8re8.v`, `EEW/8 = 1` byte, so the alignment requirement is at least `SEWMIN/8` bytes.  

- **Data Layout**  
  - Because in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. The EEW=8 encoding serves as a hint that the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW.  

- **Effect on Architectural State**  
  - The instruction **does not modify `vl` or `vtype`**.  
  - It loads exactly `8 * VLEN/8` bytes from memory into registers v8‑v15.  

- **Reservation Conditions**  
  - The instruction encoding is reserved if any of the following hold:  
    - `nf` is not one of the supported values (1, 2, 4, 8).  
    - The vector register numbers are not aligned as a vector register group.  
    - `vstart ≥ evl`.

## 31.7.9. Vector Load/Store Whole Register Instructions

Format for Vector Load Whole Register Instructions under LOAD-FP major opcode

<image>

Format for Vector Store Whole Register Instructions under STORE-FP major opcode

<image>

These instructions load and store whole vector register groups.

<image>

These instructions are intended to be used to save and restore vector registers when the type or length of the current contents of the vector register is not known, or where modifying vl and vtype would be costly. Examples include compiler register spills, vector function calls where values are passed in vector registers, interrupt handlers, and OS context switches. Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the vlenb register.

The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit-stride loads.

<image>

Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . ```

<image>

**VL8RE32.V – whole‑register vector load of eight registers, EEW = 32 bits**

- **Pseudocode name** – The assembly mnemonic `vl8re32.v v8, (a0)` is a pseudoinstruction that expands to the actual instruction `vl8re32.v v8, (a0)`. It loads the vector register group **v8‑v15** from memory starting at the address contained in scalar register **a0**.

- **Encoding fields**
  - The **nf** field encodes the number of registers to transfer. For VL8RE32.V, `NFIELDS = 8`.  
  - The **EEW** (encoded element width) is 32 bits (4 bytes).  
  - The **mew** and **width** fields encode EEW in the same pattern as regular unit‑stride loads.

- **Register‑group alignment**
  - The encoded number of registers **must be a power of 2** and the vector register numbers **must be aligned as with a vector register group**, otherwise the instruction encoding is **reserved**.  
  - Only `NFIELDS` values of **1, 2, 4, 8** are supported; other values are reserved. VL8RE32.V uses the supported value 8.

- **Memory layout**
  - When multiple registers are transferred, **the lowest‑numbered vector register is held in the lowest‑numbered memory addresses** and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.  
  - Thus the bytes for `v8` occupy the first `VLEN/8` bytes, those for `v9` the next `VLEN/8` bytes, and so on up to `v15`.

- **Effective vector length (evl)**
  - The instruction operates with an **effective vector length**  
    ```
    evl = NFIELDS * VLEN / EEW
    ```  
    For VL8RE32.V: `evl = 8 * VLEN / 32`.  
  - This evl is used **instead of the current `vl` and `vtype` settings**.

- **vstart handling**
  - The usual property *"no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl"* **does not apply** to VL8RE32.V.  
  - The instruction is **reserved** if `vstart ≥ evl`.  

- **Base address**
  - The base address is taken from the **scalar integer register specified by `rs1`** (the register named in the assembly syntax, e.g., `a0`).  
  - The instruction operates **similarly to an unmasked unit‑stride load**.

- **Misaligned address exception**
  - Implementations **are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception** on whole‑register loads if the base address is **not naturally aligned** to the larger of:
    1. the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (`EEW/8` = 4 bytes for VL8RE32.V), or  
    2. the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (`SEWMIN/8`).  
  - Some implementations may also raise the exception for the smallest supported SEW even when that SEW is larger than the encoded EEW.  

- **Exception and reservation summary for VL8RE32.V**
  - **Reserved** if any of the following holds:
    - `NFIELDS` is not 1, 2, 4, or 8, or not a power of 2.  
    - Vector register numbers are not aligned as a vector register group.  
    - `vstart ≥ evl`.  
  - **May raise** a misaligned address exception if the base address alignment requirement described above is not met.

## 31.7.9. Vector Load/Store Whole Register Instructions

Format for Vector Load Whole Register Instructions under LOAD-FP major opcode

<image>

Format for Vector Store Whole Register Instructions under STORE-FP major opcode

<image>

These instructions load and store whole vector register groups.

<image>

These instructions are intended to be used to save and restore vector registers when the type or length of the current contents of the vector register is not known, or where modifying vl and vtype would be costly. Examples include compiler register spills, vector function calls where values are passed in vector registers, interrupt handlers, and OS context switches. Software can determine the number of bytes transferred by reading the vlenb register.

The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit-stride loads.

<image>

Because  in-register  byte  layouts  are  identical  to  in-memory  byte  layouts,  the  same  data  is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW. Hence, it would have sufficed to provide  only  EEW=8 variants.  The  full  set  of  EEW  variants  is  provided  so  that  the  encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW, which aids implementations that rearrange data internally.

The vector whole register store instructions are encoded similar to unmasked unit-stride store of elements with EEW=8.

The nf field  encodes  how  many  vector  registers  to  load  and  store  using  the  NFIELDS  encoding  (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. NFIELDS indicates the number of vector registers to transfer, numbered successively after the base. Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2,  4,  8  are  supported,  with  other  values  reserved.  When  multiple  registers  are  transferred,  the  lowestnumbered vector register is held in the lowest-numbered memory addresses and successive vector register numbers are placed contiguously in memory.

The instructions operate with an effective vector length, evl =NFIELDS*VLEN/EEW, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl . The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply to these instructions. Similarly, the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply. Instead, the instructions are reserved if vstart

```
≥ evl .
```

The  instructions  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  unit-stride  load  and  store  instructions,  with  the  base address passed in the scalar x register specified by rs1 .

Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (EEW/8) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (SEWMIN/8).

<image>

Allowing  misaligned  exceptions  to  be  raised  based  on  non-alignment  to  the  encoded  EEW simplifies the implementation of these instructions. Some subset implementations might not support smaller SEW widths, so are allowed to report misaligned exceptions for the smallest supported SEW even if larger than encoded EEW. An extreme non-standard implementation might  have  SEWMIN >XLEN for  example.  Software  environments  can  mandate  the  minimum alignment requirements to support an ABI.

```
# Format of whole register load and store instructions. vl1r.v v3, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl1re8.v vl1re8.v    v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/8 bytes held at address in a0 vl1re16.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl1re32.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl1re64.v   v3, (a0)  # Load v3 with VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl2r.v v2, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl2re8.v vl2re8.v    v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl2re16.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/16 halfwords held at address in a0 vl2re32.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/32 words held at address in a0 vl2re64.v   v2, (a0)  # Load v2-v3 with 2*VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0 vl4r.v v4, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl4re8.v vl4re8.v    v4, (a0)  # Load v4-v7 with 4*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl4re16.v   v4, (a0) vl4re32.v   v4, (a0) vl4re64.v   v4, (a0) vl8r.v v8, (a0)       # Pseudoinstruction equal to vl8re8.v vl8re8.v    v8, (a0)  # Load v8-v15 with 8*VLEN/8 bytes from address in a0 vl8re16.v   v8, (a0) vl8re32.v   v8, (a0) vl8re64.v   v8, (a0) vs1r.v v3, (a1)      # Store v3 to address in a1 vs2r.v v2, (a1)      # Store v2-v3 to address in a1 vs4r.v v4, (a1)      # Store v4-v7 to address in a1
```

## vs8r.v v8, (a1)      # Store v8-v15 to address in a1

<image>

We have considered adding a whole register mask load instruction ( vl1rm.v ) but have decided to omit from initial extension. The primary purpose would be to inform the microarchitecture that the data will be used as a mask. The same effect can be achieved with the following code sequence, whose cost is at most four instructions. Of these, the first could likely be removed as vl is often already in a scalar register, and the last might already be present if the following vector instruction needs a new SEW/LMUL. So, in best case only two instructions (of which only  one  performs  vector  operations)  are  needed  to  synthesize  the  effect  of  the  dedicated instruction:

```
csrr t0, vl                        # Save current vl (potentially not needed) vsetvli t1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma     # Maximum VLMAX vlm.v v0, (a0)                     # Load mask register vsetvli x0, t0, <new type>         # Restore vl (potentially already present)
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Encoding and EEW**  
  The load instructions have an EEW encoded in the mew and width fields following the pattern of regular unit‑stride loads. For **vl8re64.v**, the encoded EEW is 64.

- **Number of registers transferred (NFIELDS)**  
  The **nf** field encodes how many vector registers to load and store using the NFIELDS encoding (Figure Table 55). The encoded number of registers must be a power of 2 and the vector register numbers must be aligned as with a vector register group, otherwise the instruction encoding is reserved. **Only NFIELDS values of 1, 2, 4, 8 are supported**, with other values reserved. For **vl8re64.v**, NFIELDS = 8, so the instruction loads registers v8–v15.

- **Effective vector length (evl)**  
  The instructions operate with an effective vector length, **evl = NFIELDS × VLEN / EEW**, regardless of current settings in vtype and vl. For **vl8re64.v**, evl = 8 × VLEN / 64.

- **Reservation condition**  
  The instructions are reserved if **vstart ≥ evl**. The usual property that no elements are written if vstart ≥ vl does not apply, and the property that the instructions are reserved if vstart exceeds the largest element index for the current vtype setting does not apply.

- **Memory layout**  
  Because **in‑register byte layouts are identical to in‑memory byte layouts, the same data is written to the destination register group regardless of EEW**. The encoded EEW can be used as a hint to indicate the destination register group will next be accessed with this EEW.

- **Base address**  
  The instructions operate similarly to unmasked unit‑stride load and store instructions, with the base address passed in the scalar x register specified by **rs1**.

- **Misaligned address exception**  
  Implementations are allowed to raise a misaligned address exception on whole register loads and stores if the base address is not naturally aligned to the larger of the size of the encoded EEW in bytes (**EEW/8**) or the implementation's smallest supported SEW size in bytes (**SEWMIN/8**).

- **Pseudocode representation**  
  ```
  vl8re64.v v8, (a0)   # Load v8‑v15 with 8*VLEN/64 doublewords held at address in a0
  ```

```
# Vector unit-stride loads and stores # vd destination, rs1 base address, vm is mask encoding (v0.t or <missing>) vle8.v    vd, (rs1), vm  #    8-bit unit-stride load vle16.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   16-bit unit-stride load
```


Additional  unit-stride  mask  load  and  store  instructions  are  provided  to  transfer  mask  values  to/from memory.  These  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  byte  loads  or  stores  (EEW=8),  except  that  the  effective vector  length  is evl =ceil( vl /8)  (i.e.  EMUL=1),  and  the  destination  register  is  always  written  with  a  tailagnostic policy.

```
# Vector unit-stride mask load vlm.v vd, (rs1)   #  Load byte vector of length ceil(vl/8) # Vector unit-stride mask store vsm.v vs3, (rs1)  #  Store byte vector of length ceil(vl/8)
```

vlm.v and vsm.v are  encoded  with  the  same width[2:0] =0  encoding  as vle8.v and vse8.v ,  but  are distinguished by different lumop and sumop encodings. Since vlm.v and vsm.v operate as byte loads and stores, vstart is in units of bytes for these instructions.

<image>

 vlm.v and vsm.v respect the vill field in vtype , as they depend on vtype indirectly through its constraints on vl .

<image>

The previous assembler mnemonics vle1.v and vse1.v were confusing as length was handled differently  for  these  instructions  versus  other  element  load/store  instructions.  To  avoid software churn, these older assembly mnemonics are being retained as aliases.

<image>

The primary motivation to provide mask load and store is to support machines that internally rearrange data to reduce cross-datapath wiring. However, these instructions also provide a convenient mechanism to use packed bit vectors in memory as mask values, and also reduce the cost of mask spill/fill by reducing need to change vl .

## 31.7.7. Unit-stride Fault-Only-First Loads

The  unit-stride  fault-only-first  load  instructions  are  used  to  vectorize  loops  with  data-dependent  exit conditions ("while" loops). These instructions execute as a regular load except that they will only take a trap caused by a synchronous exception on element 0. If element 0 raises an exception, vl is not modified, and the trap is taken. If an element > 0 raises an exception, the corresponding trap is not taken, and the vector length vl is reduced to the index of the element that would have raised an exception.

Load instructions may overwrite active destination vector register group elements past the element index at  which  the  trap  is  reported.  Similarly,  fault-only-first  load  instructions  may  update  active  destination elements  past  the  element  that  causes  trimming  of  the  vector  length  (but  not  past  the  original  vector length). The values of these spurious updates do not have to correspond to the values in memory at the addressed memory locations. Non-idempotent memory locations can only be accessed when it is known the corresponding element load operation will not be restarted due to a trap or vector-length trimming.

```
# Vector unit-stride fault-only-first loads # vd destination, rs1 base address, vm is mask encoding (v0.t or <missing>) vle8ff.v    vd, (rs1), vm  #    8-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle16ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   16-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle32ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   32-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle64ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   64-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load
```

```
strlen example using unit-stride fault-only-first instruction # size_t strlen(const char *str) # a0 holds *str strlen: mv a3, a0             # Save start loop:
```

```
vsetvli a1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma  # Vector of bytes of maximum length vle8ff.v v8, (a3)      # Load bytes csrr a1, vl           # Get bytes read vmseq.vi v0, v8, 0    # Set v0[i] where v8[i] = 0 vfirst.m a2, v0       # Find first set bit add a3, a3, a1        # Bump pointer bltz a2, loop         # Not found? add a0, a0, a1        # Sum start + bump add a3, a3, a2        # Add index sub a0, a3, a0        # Subtract start address+bump ret
```

<image>

There is  a  security  concern  with  fault-on-first  loads,  as  they  can  be  used  to  probe  for  valid effective addresses. The unit-stride versions only allow probing a  region  immediately contiguous to a known region, and so reduce the security impact when used in unprivileged code. However, code running in S-mode can establish arbitrary page translations that allow probing  of  random  guest  physical  addresses  provided  by  a  hypervisor.  Constant-stride  and scatter/gather fault-only-first instructions are not provided due to lack of encoding space, but they  can  also  represent  a  larger  security  hole,  allowing  even  unprivileged  software  to  easily check multiple random pages for accessibility without experiencing a trap. This standard does not address possible security mitigations for fault-only-first instructions.

Even when an exception is not raised, implementations are permitted to process fewer than vl elements and reduce vl accordingly, but if vstart =0 and vl >0, then at least one element must be processed.

When the fault-only-first instruction takes a trap due to an interrupt, implementations should not reduce vl and should instead set a vstart value.

<image>

When  the  fault-only-first  instruction  would  trigger  a  debug  data-watchpoint  trap  on  an element after the first, implementations should not reduce vl but instead should trigger the debug trap as otherwise the event might be lost.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
These unit‑stride fault‑only‑first load instructions, including **vle8ff.v**, have the following architectural behavior:

- They **execute as a regular load** except that they **will only take a trap caused by a synchronous exception on element 0**.  
- **If element 0 raises an exception**, **vl is not modified**, and the trap is taken.  
- **If an element > 0 raises an exception**, the corresponding trap is **not taken**, and the **vector length vl is reduced to the index of the element that would have raised an exception**.  
- **Load instructions may overwrite active destination vector‑register‑group elements past the element index at which the trap is reported.**  
- **Similarly, fault‑only‑first load instructions may update active destination elements past the element that causes trimming of the vector length (but not past the original vector length).**  
- **The values of these spurious updates do not have to correspond to the values in memory at the addressed memory locations.**  
- **Non‑idempotent memory locations can only be accessed when it is known the corresponding element load operation will not be restarted due to a trap or vector‑length trimming.**  
- **Even when an exception is not raised, implementations are permitted to process fewer than vl elements and reduce vl accordingly, but if vstart = 0 and vl > 0, then at least one element must be processed.**  
- **When the fault‑only‑first instruction takes a trap due to an interrupt, implementations should not reduce vl and should instead set a vstart value.**  
- **When the fault‑only‑first instruction would trigger a debug data‑watchpoint trap on an element after the first, implementations should not reduce vl but instead should trigger the debug trap as otherwise the event might be lost.**

## 31.7.7. Unit-stride Fault-Only-First Loads

The  unit-stride  fault-only-first  load  instructions  are  used  to  vectorize  loops  with  data-dependent  exit conditions ("while" loops). These instructions execute as a regular load except that they will only take a trap caused by a synchronous exception on element 0. If element 0 raises an exception, vl is not modified, and the trap is taken. If an element > 0 raises an exception, the corresponding trap is not taken, and the vector length vl is reduced to the index of the element that would have raised an exception.

Load instructions may overwrite active destination vector register group elements past the element index at  which  the  trap  is  reported.  Similarly,  fault-only-first  load  instructions  may  update  active  destination elements  past  the  element  that  causes  trimming  of  the  vector  length  (but  not  past  the  original  vector length). The values of these spurious updates do not have to correspond to the values in memory at the addressed memory locations. Non-idempotent memory locations can only be accessed when it is known the corresponding element load operation will not be restarted due to a trap or vector-length trimming.

```
# Vector unit-stride fault-only-first loads # vd destination, rs1 base address, vm is mask encoding (v0.t or <missing>) vle8ff.v    vd, (rs1), vm  #    8-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle16ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   16-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle32ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   32-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle64ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   64-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load
```

```
strlen example using unit-stride fault-only-first instruction # size_t strlen(const char *str) # a0 holds *str strlen: mv a3, a0             # Save start loop:
```

```
vsetvli a1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma  # Vector of bytes of maximum length vle8ff.v v8, (a3)      # Load bytes csrr a1, vl           # Get bytes read vmseq.vi v0, v8, 0    # Set v0[i] where v8[i] = 0 vfirst.m a2, v0       # Find first set bit add a3, a3, a1        # Bump pointer bltz a2, loop         # Not found? add a0, a0, a1        # Sum start + bump add a3, a3, a2        # Add index sub a0, a3, a0        # Subtract start address+bump ret
```

<image>

There is  a  security  concern  with  fault-on-first  loads,  as  they  can  be  used  to  probe  for  valid effective addresses. The unit-stride versions only allow probing a  region  immediately contiguous to a known region, and so reduce the security impact when used in unprivileged code. However, code running in S-mode can establish arbitrary page translations that allow probing  of  random  guest  physical  addresses  provided  by  a  hypervisor.  Constant-stride  and scatter/gather fault-only-first instructions are not provided due to lack of encoding space, but they  can  also  represent  a  larger  security  hole,  allowing  even  unprivileged  software  to  easily check multiple random pages for accessibility without experiencing a trap. This standard does not address possible security mitigations for fault-only-first instructions.

Even when an exception is not raised, implementations are permitted to process fewer than vl elements and reduce vl accordingly, but if vstart =0 and vl >0, then at least one element must be processed.

When the fault-only-first instruction takes a trap due to an interrupt, implementations should not reduce vl and should instead set a vstart value.

<image>

When  the  fault-only-first  instruction  would  trigger  a  debug  data-watchpoint  trap  on  an element after the first, implementations should not reduce vl but instead should trigger the debug trap as otherwise the event might be lost.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:

## 31.7.4. Vector Unit-Stride Instructions

```
# Vector unit-stride loads and stores # vd destination, rs1 base address, vm is mask encoding (v0.t or <missing>) vle8.v    vd, (rs1), vm  #    8-bit unit-stride load vle16.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   16-bit unit-stride load
```

```
vle32.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   32-bit unit-stride load vle64.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   64-bit unit-stride load # vs3 store data, rs1 base address, vm is mask encoding (v0.t or <missing>) vse8.v    vs3, (rs1), vm  #    8-bit unit-stride store vse16.v   vs3, (rs1), vm  #   16-bit unit-stride store vse32.v   vs3, (rs1), vm  #   32-bit unit-stride store vse64.v   vs3, (rs1), vm  #   64-bit unit-stride store
```

Additional  unit-stride  mask  load  and  store  instructions  are  provided  to  transfer  mask  values  to/from memory.  These  operate  similarly  to  unmasked  byte  loads  or  stores  (EEW=8),  except  that  the  effective vector  length  is evl =ceil( vl /8)  (i.e.  EMUL=1),  and  the  destination  register  is  always  written  with  a  tailagnostic policy.

```
# Vector unit-stride mask load vlm.v vd, (rs1)   #  Load byte vector of length ceil(vl/8) # Vector unit-stride mask store vsm.v vs3, (rs1)  #  Store byte vector of length ceil(vl/8)
```

vlm.v and vsm.v are  encoded  with  the  same width[2:0] =0  encoding  as vle8.v and vse8.v ,  but  are distinguished by different lumop and sumop encodings. Since vlm.v and vsm.v operate as byte loads and stores, vstart is in units of bytes for these instructions.

<image>

 vlm.v and vsm.v respect the vill field in vtype , as they depend on vtype indirectly through its constraints on vl .

<image>

The previous assembler mnemonics vle1.v and vse1.v were confusing as length was handled differently  for  these  instructions  versus  other  element  load/store  instructions.  To  avoid software churn, these older assembly mnemonics are being retained as aliases.

<image>

The primary motivation to provide mask load and store is to support machines that internally rearrange data to reduce cross-datapath wiring. However, these instructions also provide a convenient mechanism to use packed bit vectors in memory as mask values, and also reduce the cost of mask spill/fill by reducing need to change vl .

- **Syntax**: `vd, (rs1), vs2, vm` where `vd` is the destination vector register, `rs1` holds the base address, `vs2` provides byte offsets, and `vm` is the optional mask.  
- **Operation**: *ordered 8‑bit indexed load of SEW data*.  
- **Assembler notation**: The assembler syntax uses the "ei" suffix (e.g., `vloxei8.v`) to indicate that the statically encoded EEW applies to the index, not to the data.  
- **Mnemonic convention**: The "O" in the mnemonic distinguishes it as an **ordered** operation; unordered indexed loads use a "U" (e.g., `vluxei8.v`).  
- **Alias behavior**: The opcode may be retained as an alias `VSXEI8.V`, which previously denoted an ordered operation; the alias has the same architectural behavior as VLOXEI8.V.

## 31.7.5. Vector Constant-Stride Instructions

```
# Vector constant-stride loads and stores # vd destination, rs1 base address, rs2 byte constant-stride vlse8.v    vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #    8-bit constant-stride load vlse16.v   vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   16-bit constant-stride load vlse32.v   vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   32-bit constant-stride load vlse64.v   vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   64-bit constant-stride load # vs3 store data, rs1 base address, rs2 byte constant-stride vsse8.v    vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #    8-bit constant-stride store vsse16.v   vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   16-bit constant-stride store
```

```
vsse32.v   vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   32-bit constant-stride store
```

```
vsse64.v   vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   64-bit constant-stride store
```

Negative and zero strides are supported.

Element accesses within a constant-stride instruction are unordered with respect to each other.

When rs2 = x0 , then an implementation is allowed, but not required, to perform fewer memory operations than  the  number  of  active  elements,  and  may  perform  different  numbers  of  memory  operations  across different dynamic executions of the same static instruction.

<image>

Compilers must be aware to not use the x0 form for rs2 when the immediate stride is 0 if the intent is to require all memory accesses are performed.

When rs2!=x0 and the value of x[rs2]=0 , the implementation must perform one memory access for each active element (but these accesses will not be ordered).

<image>

As with other architectural mandates, implementations must appear to perform each memory access. Microarchitectures are free to optimize away accesses that would not be observed by another  agent,  for  example,  in  idempotent  memory  regions  obeying  RVWMO.  For  nonidempotent memory regions, where by definition each access can be observed by a device, the optimization would not be possible.

<image>

When repeating ordered vector accesses to the same memory address are required, then an ordered indexed operation can be used.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Syntax**  
  ```
  vlse8.v    vd, (rs1), rs2, vm   # 8‑bit constant‑stride load
  ```

- **Supported stride values**  
  *Negative and zero strides are supported.*

- **Ordering of element accesses**  
  *Element accesses within a constant‑stride instruction are unordered with respect to each other.*

- **Behavior when `rs2 = x0` (zero‑stride form)**  
  *When `rs2 = x0`, an implementation is allowed, but not required, to perform fewer memory operations than the number of active elements, and may perform different numbers of memory operations across different dynamic executions of the same static instruction.*

- **Compiler guidance for zero‑stride form**  
  *Compilers must be aware to not use the `x0` form for `rs2` when the immediate stride is 0 if the intent is to require all memory accesses are performed.*

- **Behavior when `rs2 != x0` and the stride value is zero**  
  *When `rs2 != x0` and the value of `x[rs2] = 0`, the implementation must perform one memory access for each active element (but these accesses will not be ordered).*

- **Visibility of memory accesses**  
  *Implementations must appear to perform each memory access.*  
  *Microarchitectures are free to optimize away accesses that would not be observed by another agent, for example, in idempotent memory regions obeying RVWMO. For non‑idempotent memory regions, where by definition each access can be observed by a device, the optimization would not be possible.*

- **Ordered accesses alternative**  
  *When repeating ordered vector accesses to the same memory address are required, then an ordered indexed operation can be used.*

```
# Vector constant-stride loads and stores # vd destination, rs1 base address, rs2 byte constant-stride vlse8.v    vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #    8-bit constant-stride load vlse16.v   vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   16-bit constant-stride load vlse32.v   vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   32-bit constant-stride load vlse64.v   vd, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   64-bit constant-stride load # vs3 store data, rs1 base address, rs2 byte constant-stride vsse8.v    vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #    8-bit constant-stride store vsse16.v   vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   16-bit constant-stride store
```

```
vsse32.v   vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   32-bit constant-stride store
```

```
vsse64.v   vs3, (rs1), rs2, vm  #   64-bit constant-stride store
```

Negative and zero strides are supported.

Element accesses within a constant-stride instruction are unordered with respect to each other.

When rs2 = x0 , then an implementation is allowed, but not required, to perform fewer memory operations than  the  number  of  active  elements,  and  may  perform  different  numbers  of  memory  operations  across different dynamic executions of the same static instruction.

<image>

Compilers must be aware to not use the x0 form for rs2 when the immediate stride is 0 if the intent is to require all memory accesses are performed.

When rs2!=x0 and the value of x[rs2]=0 , the implementation must perform one memory access for each active element (but these accesses will not be ordered).

<image>

As with other architectural mandates, implementations must appear to perform each memory access. Microarchitectures are free to optimize away accesses that would not be observed by another  agent,  for  example,  in  idempotent  memory  regions  obeying  RVWMO.  For  nonidempotent memory regions, where by definition each access can be observed by a device, the optimization would not be possible.

<image>

When repeating ordered vector accesses to the same memory address are required, then an ordered indexed operation can be used.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
