## 31.11.4. Vector Integer Add-with-Carry / Subtract-with-Borrow Instructions

To support multi-word integer arithmetic, instructions that operate on a carry bit are provided. For each operation (add or subtract), two instructions are provided: one to provide the result (SEW width), and the second to generate the carry output (single bit encoded as a mask boolean).

The carry inputs and outputs are represented using the mask register layout as described in Section 31.4.5. Due to encoding constraints, the carry input must come from the implicit v0 register, but carry outputs can be written to any vector register that respects the source/destination overlap restrictions.

vadc and vsbc add or subtract the source operands and the carry-in or borrow-in, and write the result to vector register vd .  These instructions are encoded as masked instructions ( vm=0 ), but they operate on and

write back all body elements. Encodings corresponding to the unmasked versions ( vm=1 ) are reserved.

vmadc and vmsbc add or subtract the source operands, optionally add the carry-in or subtract the borrow-in if  masked ( vm=0 ),  and  write  the  resulting  carry-out  or  borrow-out back to mask register vd .  If  unmasked ( vm=1 ), there is no carry-in or borrow-in. These instructions operate on and write back all body elements, even if masked. Because these instructions produce a mask value, they always operate with a tail-agnostic policy.

```
# Produce sum with carry. # vd[i] = vs2[i] + vs1[i] + v0.mask[i] vadc.vvm   vd, vs2, vs1, v0  # Vector-vector # vd[i] = vs2[i] + x[rs1] + v0.mask[i] vadc.vxm   vd, vs2, rs1, v0  # Vector-scalar # vd[i] = vs2[i] + imm + v0.mask[i] vadc.vim   vd, vs2, imm, v0  # Vector-immediate # Produce carry out in mask register format # vd.mask[i] = carry_out(vs2[i] + vs1[i] + v0.mask[i]) vmadc.vvm   vd, vs2, vs1, v0  # Vector-vector # vd.mask[i] = carry_out(vs2[i] + x[rs1] + v0.mask[i]) vmadc.vxm   vd, vs2, rs1, v0  # Vector-scalar # vd.mask[i] = carry_out(vs2[i] + imm + v0.mask[i]) vmadc.vim   vd, vs2, imm, v0  # Vector-immediate # vd.mask[i] = carry_out(vs2[i] + vs1[i]) vmadc.vv    vd, vs2, vs1      # Vector-vector, no carry-in # vd.mask[i] = carry_out(vs2[i] + x[rs1]) vmadc.vx    vd, vs2, rs1      # Vector-scalar, no carry-in # vd.mask[i] = carry_out(vs2[i] + imm) vmadc.vi    vd, vs2, imm      # Vector-immediate, no carry-in
```

Because  implementing  a  carry  propagation  requires  executing  two  instructions  with  unchanged  inputs, destructive accumulations will require an additional move to obtain correct results.

```
# Example multi-word arithmetic sequence, accumulating into v4 vmadc.vvm v1, v4, v8, v0  # Get carry into temp register v1 vadc.vvm v4, v4, v8, v0   # Calc new sum vmmv.m v0, v1             # Move temp carry into v0 for next word
```

The  subtract  with  borrow  instruction vsbc performs  the  equivalent  function  to  support  long  word

arithmetic for subtraction. There are no subtract with immediate instructions.

```
# Produce difference with borrow. # vd[i] = vs2[i] - vs1[i] - v0.mask[i] vsbc.vvm   vd, vs2, vs1, v0  # Vector-vector # vd[i] = vs2[i] - x[rs1] - v0.mask[i] vsbc.vxm   vd, vs2, rs1, v0  # Vector-scalar # Produce borrow out in mask register format # vd.mask[i] = borrow_out(vs2[i] - vs1[i] - v0.mask[i]) vmsbc.vvm   vd, vs2, vs1, v0  # Vector-vector # vd.mask[i] = borrow_out(vs2[i] - x[rs1] - v0.mask[i]) vmsbc.vxm   vd, vs2, rs1, v0  # Vector-scalar # vd.mask[i] = borrow_out(vs2[i] - vs1[i]) vmsbc.vv    vd, vs2, vs1      # Vector-vector, no borrow-in # vd.mask[i] = borrow_out(vs2[i] - x[rs1]) vmsbc.vx    vd, vs2, rs1      # Vector-scalar, no borrow-in
```

For vmsbc , the borrow is defined to be 1 iff the difference, prior to truncation, is negative.

For vadc and vsbc , the instruction encoding is reserved if the destination vector register is v0 .

## 31.3.4.3. Vector Tail Agnostic and Vector Mask Agnostic vta and vma

These  two  bits  modify  the  behavior  of  destination  tail  elements  and  destination  inactive  masked-off elements  respectively  during  the  execution  of  vector  instructions.  The  tail  and  inactive  sets  contain element positions that are not receiving new results during a vector operation, as defined in Section 31.5.4.

All systems must support all four options:

|   vta |   vma | Tail Elements   | Inactive Elements   |
|-------|-------|-----------------|---------------------|
|     0 |     0 | undisturbed     | undisturbed         |
|     0 |     1 | undisturbed     | agnostic            |
|     1 |     0 | agnostic        | undisturbed         |
|     1 |     1 | agnostic        | agnostic            |

Mask destination tail elements are always treated as tail-agnostic, regardless of the setting of vta .

When a set is marked undisturbed, the corresponding set of destination elements in a vector register group retain the value they previously held.

When a set is marked agnostic, the corresponding set of destination elements in any vector destination operand can either retain the value they previously held, or are overwritten with 1s. Within a single vector instruction,  each  destination  element  can  be  either  left  undisturbed  or  overwritten  with  1s,  in  any combination,  and  the  pattern  of  undisturbed  or  overwritten  with  1s  is  not  required  to  be  deterministic when the instruction is executed with the same inputs.

<image>

The agnostic policy was added to accommodate machines with vector register renaming. With an undisturbed policy, all elements would have to be read from the old physical destination vector register to be copied into the new physical destination vector register. This causes an inefficiency when these inactive or tail values are not required for subsequent calculations.

<image>

The value of all 1s instead of all 0s was chosen for the overwrite value to discourage software developers from depending on the value written.

<image>

<image>

<image>

A  simple  in-order  implementation  can  ignore  the  settings  and  simply  execute  all  vector instructions using the undisturbed policy. The vta and vma state bits must still be provided in vtype for compatibility and to support thread migration.

An out-of-order implementation can choose to implement tail-agnostic + mask-agnostic using tail-agnostic + mask-undisturbed to reduce implementation complexity.

The  definition  of  agnostic  result  policy  is  left  loose  to  accommodate  migrating  application threads  between  harts  on  a  small  in-order  core  (which  probably  leaves  agnostic  regions undisturbed) and harts on a larger out-of-order core with register renaming (which probably overwrites  agnostic  elements  with  1s).  As  it  might  be  necessary  to  restart  in  the  middle,  we allow  arbitrary  mixing  of  agnostic  policies  within  a  single  vector  instruction.  This  allowed mixing  of  policies  also  enables  implementations  that  might  change  policies  for  different granules of a vector register, for example, using undisturbed within a granule that is actively operated on but renaming to all 1s for granules in the tail.

In addition, except for mask load instructions, any element in the tail of a mask result can also be written with  the  value  the  mask-producing  operation  would  have  calculated  with vl =VLMAX. Furthermore, for mask-logical instructions and vmsbf.m , vmsif.m , vmsof.m mask-manipulation instructions, any element in the tail of the result can be written with the value the mask-producing operation would have calculated with vl =VLEN, SEW=8, and LMUL=8 (i.e., all bits of the mask register can be overwritten).

<image>

Mask tails are always treated as agnostic to reduce complexity of managing mask data, which can  be  written  at  bit  granularity.  There  appears  to  be  little  software  need  to  support  tailundisturbed for mask register values. Allowing mask-generating instructions to write back the result  of  the  instruction  avoids  the  need  for  logic  to  mask  out  the  tail,  except  mask  loads cannot write memory values to destination mask tails as this would imply accessing memory past software intent.

The assembly syntax adds two mandatory flags to the vsetvli instruction:

```
ta   # Tail agnostic tu   # Tail undisturbed ma   # Mask agnostic mu   # Mask undisturbed vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, ta, ma   # Tail agnostic, mask agnostic vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, tu, ma   # Tail undisturbed, mask agnostic vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, ta, mu   # Tail agnostic, mask undisturbed vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, tu, mu   # Tail undisturbed, mask undisturbed
```

<image>

Prior  to  v0.9,  when  these  flags  were  not  specified  on  a vsetvli ,  they  defaulted  to  maskundisturbed/tail-undisturbed. - Mask tails are always treated as **agnostic** to reduce complexity of managing mask data, which can be written at bit granularity.

- Mask destination tail elements are always treated as **tail‑agnostic**, regardless of the setting of the **vta** bit.

## 31.15.4. vmsbf.m set-before-first mask bit

```
vmsbf.m vd, vs2, vm # Example 7 6 5 4 3 2 1 0   Element number 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 0   v3 contents vmsbf.m v2, v3 0 0 0 0 0 0 1 1   v2 contents 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 1   v3 contents vmsbf.m v2, v3 0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0   v2
```

```
0 0 0 0 0 0 0 0   v3 contents vmsbf.m v2, v3 1 1 1 1 1 1 1 1   v2 1 1 0 0 0 0 1 1   v0 vcontents 1 0 0 1 0 1 0 0   v3 contents vmsbf.m v2, v3, v0.t 0 1 x x x x 1 1   v2 contents
```

The vmsbf.m instruction takes a mask register as input and writes results to a mask register. The instruction writes a 1 to all active mask elements before the first active source element that is a 1, then writes a 0 to that element and all following active elements. If there is no set bit in the active elements of the source vector, then all active elements in the destination are written with a 1.

The tail elements in the destination mask register are updated under a tail-agnostic policy.

Traps  on vmsbf.m are  always  reported  with  a vstart of  0.  The vmsbf instruction  will  raise  an  illegalinstruction exception if vstart is non-zero.

The destination register cannot overlap the source register and, if masked, cannot overlap the mask register ('v0').

## 31.15.7. Example using vector mask instructions

The following is an example of vectorizing a data-dependent exit loop.

```
# char* strcpy(char *dst, const char* src) strcpy: mv a2, a0             # Copy dst li t0, -1             # Infinite AVL loop: vsetvli x0, t0, e8, m8, ta, ma  # Max length vectors of bytes vle8ff.v v8, (a1)        # Get src bytes csrr t1, vl           # Get number of bytes fetched
```

```
vmseq.vi v1, v8, 0      # Flag zero bytes vfirst.m a3, v1         # Zero found? add a1, a1, t1        # Bump pointer vmsif.m v0, v1          # Set mask up to and including zero byte. vse8.v v8, (a2), v0.t    # Write out bytes add a2, a2, t1        # Bump pointer bltz a3, loop         # Zero byte not found, so loop ret
```

```
# char* strncpy(char *dst, const char* src, size_t n) strncpy: mv a3, a0             # Copy dst loop: vsetvli x0, a2, e8, m8, ta, ma   # Vectors of bytes. vle8ff.v v8, (a1)        # Get src bytes vmseq.vi v1, v8, 0      # Flag zero bytes csrr t1, vl           # Get number of bytes fetched vfirst.m a4, v1         # Zero found? vmsbf.m v0, v1          # Set mask up to before zero byte. vse8.v v8, (a3), v0.t    # Write out non-zero bytes bgez a4, zero_tail    # Zero remaining bytes. sub a2, a2, t1        # Decrement count. add a3, a3, t1        # Bump dest pointer add a1, a1, t1        # Bump src pointer bnez a2, loop         # Anymore? ret zero_tail: sub a2, a2, a4          # Subtract count on non-zero bytes. add a3, a3, a4          # Advance past non-zero bytes. vsetvli t1, a2, e8, m8, ta, ma   # Vectors of bytes. vmv.v.i v0, 0           # Splat zero. zero_loop: vse8.v v0, (a3)          # Store zero. sub a2, a2, t1        # Decrement count. add a3, a3, t1        # Bump pointer vsetvli t1, a2, e8, m8, ta, ma   # Vectors of bytes. bnez a2, zero_loop    # Anymore? ret
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Instruction:** `vmsbf.m vd, vs2`  
- **Behavior:** Sets the destination mask register `vd` to true for vector elements **up to but not including** the first true element of the source mask register `vs2`. In the example, `vmsbf.m v0, v1` is used after `v1` has been generated by `vmseq.vi v1, v8, 0` (which flags zero bytes), and the comment explicitly states that the instruction "Set mask up to before zero byte." This implies that `v0` will have mask bits true for all elements preceding the first zero‑byte flag in `v1`, and false for that element and all subsequent elements.

## 31.7.7. Unit-stride Fault-Only-First Loads

The  unit-stride  fault-only-first  load  instructions  are  used  to  vectorize  loops  with  data-dependent  exit conditions ("while" loops). These instructions execute as a regular load except that they will only take a trap caused by a synchronous exception on element 0. If element 0 raises an exception, vl is not modified, and the trap is taken. If an element > 0 raises an exception, the corresponding trap is not taken, and the vector length vl is reduced to the index of the element that would have raised an exception.

Load instructions may overwrite active destination vector register group elements past the element index at  which  the  trap  is  reported.  Similarly,  fault-only-first  load  instructions  may  update  active  destination elements  past  the  element  that  causes  trimming  of  the  vector  length  (but  not  past  the  original  vector length). The values of these spurious updates do not have to correspond to the values in memory at the addressed memory locations. Non-idempotent memory locations can only be accessed when it is known the corresponding element load operation will not be restarted due to a trap or vector-length trimming.

```
# Vector unit-stride fault-only-first loads # vd destination, rs1 base address, vm is mask encoding (v0.t or <missing>) vle8ff.v    vd, (rs1), vm  #    8-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle16ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   16-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle32ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   32-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load vle64ff.v   vd, (rs1), vm  #   64-bit unit-stride fault-only-first load
```

```
strlen example using unit-stride fault-only-first instruction # size_t strlen(const char *str) # a0 holds *str strlen: mv a3, a0             # Save start loop:
```

```
vsetvli a1, x0, e8, m8, ta, ma  # Vector of bytes of maximum length vle8ff.v v8, (a3)      # Load bytes csrr a1, vl           # Get bytes read vmseq.vi v0, v8, 0    # Set v0[i] where v8[i] = 0 vfirst.m a2, v0       # Find first set bit add a3, a3, a1        # Bump pointer bltz a2, loop         # Not found? add a0, a0, a1        # Sum start + bump add a3, a3, a2        # Add index sub a0, a3, a0        # Subtract start address+bump ret
```

<image>

There is  a  security  concern  with  fault-on-first  loads,  as  they  can  be  used  to  probe  for  valid effective addresses. The unit-stride versions only allow probing a  region  immediately contiguous to a known region, and so reduce the security impact when used in unprivileged code. However, code running in S-mode can establish arbitrary page translations that allow probing  of  random  guest  physical  addresses  provided  by  a  hypervisor.  Constant-stride  and scatter/gather fault-only-first instructions are not provided due to lack of encoding space, but they  can  also  represent  a  larger  security  hole,  allowing  even  unprivileged  software  to  easily check multiple random pages for accessibility without experiencing a trap. This standard does not address possible security mitigations for fault-only-first instructions.

Even when an exception is not raised, implementations are permitted to process fewer than vl elements and reduce vl accordingly, but if vstart =0 and vl >0, then at least one element must be processed.

When the fault-only-first instruction takes a trap due to an interrupt, implementations should not reduce vl and should instead set a vstart value.

<image>

When  the  fault-only-first  instruction  would  trigger  a  debug  data-watchpoint  trap  on  an element after the first, implementations should not reduce vl but instead should trigger the debug trap as otherwise the event might be lost.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
vmseq.vi v0, v8, 0    # Set v0[i] where v8[i] = 0

## 31.11.8. Vector Integer Compare Instructions

The  following  integer  compare  instructions  write  1  to  the  destination  mask  register  element  if  the comparison  evaluates  to  true,  and  0  otherwise.  The  destination  mask  vector  is  always  held  in  a  single vector  register,  with  a  layout  of  elements  as  described  in  Section  31.4.5.  The  destination  mask  vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register ( v0 ).

```
# Set if equal vmseq.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmseq.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmseq.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if not equal vmsne.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsne.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsne.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if less than, unsigned vmsltu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsltu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # Vector-scalar # Set if less than, signed vmslt.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmslt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar # Set if less than or equal, unsigned vmsleu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm   # Vector-vector vmsleu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # vector-scalar vmsleu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if less than or equal, signed vmsle.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsle.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsle.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if greater than, unsigned vmsgtu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # Vector-scalar vmsgtu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if greater than, signed vmsgt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar vmsgt.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm    # Vector-immediate # Following two instructions are not provided directly # Set if greater than or equal, unsigned # vmsgeu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar # Set if greater than or equal, signed # vmsge.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar
```

The following table indicates how all comparisons are implemented in native machine code.

| Comparison                           | Assembler Mapping                                                                                           | Assembler Pseudoinstruction                           |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| va < vb va <= vb va > vb va >= vb    | vmslt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmslt{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm | vmsgt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsge{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm |
| va < x va <= x va > x va >= x va < i | vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsle{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm see below vm                  | vmslt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| va <= i va > i va >= i va, vb x      | vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vm    | vmsge{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| i                                    | vector register groups scalar integer register immediate                                                    |                                                       |

<image>

The  immediate  forms  of vmslt{u}.vi are  not  provided  as  the  immediate  value  can  be decreased by 1 and the vmsle{u}.vi variants used instead. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Because the 5-bit vector immediates are always sign-extended, when the high bit of the simm5 immediate is set, vmsleu.vi also supports unsigned immediate values in the range 2 SEW -16 to 2 SEW -1 ,  allowing  corresponding vmsltu.vi compares  against  unsigned  immediates  in  the range 2 SEW -15 to 2 SEW . Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```
unmasked va >= x pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x; vmnand.mm vd, vd, vd masked va >= x, vd != v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t; vmxor.mm vd, vd, v0 masked va >= x, vd == v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, vt masked va >= x, any vd pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vt, v0, vt;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, v0;  vmor.mm vd, vt, vd The vt argument to the pseudoinstruction must name a temporary vector register that is not same as vd and which will be clobbered by the pseudoinstruction
```

Compares effectively AND in the mask under a mask-undisturbed policy if the destination register is v0 , e.g.,

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask-undisturbed vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
```

Compares write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail-agnostic policy.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
The integer compare instructions, including **vmseq.vi**, "write 1 to the destination mask register element if the comparison evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise."  

The destination mask vector is "always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5." The destination mask vector register "may be the same as the source vector mask register (v0)."

**Syntax**  
```
vmseq.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # vector‑immediate
```  

All compare instructions "write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail‑agnostic policy."  

When the destination register is **v0**, compare instructions "effectively AND in the mask under a mask‑undisturbed policy."   (e.g., `vmslt.vv v0, va, vb` followed by `vmslt.vv v0, vb, vc, v0.t`).

# Set if equal vmseq.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmseq.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmseq.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if not equal vmsne.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsne.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsne.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if less than, unsigned vmsltu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsltu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # Vector-scalar # Set if less than, signed vmslt.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmslt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar # Set if less than or equal, unsigned vmsleu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm   # Vector-vector vmsleu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # vector-scalar vmsleu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if less than or equal, signed vmsle.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsle.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsle.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if greater than, unsigned vmsgtu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # Vector-scalar vmsgtu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if greater than, signed vmsgt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar vmsgt.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm    # Vector-immediate # Following two instructions are not provided directly # Set if greater than or equal, unsigned # vmsgeu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar # Set if greater than or equal, signed # vmsge.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar
```

The following table indicates how all comparisons are implemented in native machine code.

| Comparison                           | Assembler Mapping                                                                                           | Assembler Pseudoinstruction                           |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| va < vb va <= vb va > vb va >= vb    | vmslt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmslt{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm | vmsgt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsge{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm |
| va < x va <= x va > x va >= x va < i | vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsle{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm see below vm                  | vmslt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| va <= i va > i va >= i va, vb x      | vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vm    | vmsge{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| i                                    | vector register groups scalar integer register immediate                                                    |                                                       |

<image>

The  immediate  forms  of vmslt{u}.vi are  not  provided  as  the  immediate  value  can  be decreased by 1 and the vmsle{u}.vi variants used instead. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Because the 5-bit vector immediates are always sign-extended, when the high bit of the simm5 immediate is set, vmsleu.vi also supports unsigned immediate values in the range 2 SEW -16 to 2 SEW -1 ,  allowing  corresponding vmsltu.vi compares  against  unsigned  immediates  in  the range 2 SEW -15 to 2 SEW . Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```
unmasked va >= x pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x; vmnand.mm vd, vd, vd masked va >= x, vd != v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t; vmxor.mm vd, vd, v0 masked va >= x, vd == v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, vt masked va >= x, any vd pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vt, v0, vt;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, v0;  vmor.mm vd, vt, vd The vt argument to the pseudoinstruction must name a temporary vector register that is not same as vd and which will be clobbered by the pseudoinstruction
```

Compares effectively AND in the mask under a mask-undisturbed policy if the destination register is v0 , e.g.,

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask-undisturbed vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
```

Compares write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail-agnostic policy.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
The integer compare instructions, including **vmseq.vv**, write **1** to each destination mask‑register element when the comparison evaluates to true and **0** otherwise.

The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5. The destination mask vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register (**v0**).

**Mask‑policy behavior**

* When the destination register is **v0**, compares effectively AND the result into the mask under a *mask‑undisturbed* policy.  
  Example (from the text):  
  ```
  # (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask‑undisturbed
  vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written
  vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
  ```

* All compare instructions, including **vmseq.vv**, write mask registers and therefore always operate under a *tail‑agnostic* policy.

- **Mnemonic and operand form**  
  `vmseq.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm`  # vector‑scalar form of the "set if equal" compare.

- **Result written to the destination mask register**  
  The instruction writes **1** to each element of the destination mask register `vd` if the comparison "`vs2` element **==** scalar `rs1`" evaluates to true, and writes **0** otherwise.

- **Destination mask register layout**  
  The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5.  
  The destination mask vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register (`v0`).

- **Tail‑agnostic policy**  
  All integer compare instructions, including `vmseq.vx`, "write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail‑agnostic policy."

- **Mask‑undisturbed behavior when the destination register is `v0`**  
  When the destination register `vd` is `v0`, compares (including `vmseq.vx`) "effectively AND in the mask under a mask‑undisturbed policy."

The integer compare instructions **write 1 to the destination mask register element if the comparison evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise**.  
The destination mask vector is **always held in a single vector register**, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5. The destination mask register may be the same as the source vector mask register (v0).

**VMSGT.VI** is the signed‑greater‑than vector‑immediate compare instruction. Its syntax is:

```
vmsgt.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector‑immediate
```

where:

* `vd` is the destination mask register.  
* `vs2` is the source vector register containing the values to be compared.  
* `imm` is a signed immediate operand.  
* `vm` is the optional mask operand.

The instruction **sets each mask element in `vd` to 1 if the signed value in the corresponding element of `vs2` is greater than the signed immediate `imm`; otherwise it sets the element to 0**.

The **vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions**.

All compare instructions, including **vmsgt.vi**, **write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail‑agnostic policy**.
====================================================== END - 1613 ======================================================

## 31.11.8. Vector Integer Compare Instructions

The  following  integer  compare  instructions  write  1  to  the  destination  mask  register  element  if  the comparison  evaluates  to  true,  and  0  otherwise.  The  destination  mask  vector  is  always  held  in  a  single vector  register,  with  a  layout  of  elements  as  described  in  Section  31.4.5.  The  destination  mask  vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register ( v0 ).

```
# Set if equal vmseq.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmseq.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmseq.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if not equal vmsne.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsne.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsne.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if less than, unsigned vmsltu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsltu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # Vector-scalar # Set if less than, signed vmslt.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmslt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar # Set if less than or equal, unsigned vmsleu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm   # Vector-vector vmsleu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # vector-scalar vmsleu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if less than or equal, signed vmsle.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsle.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsle.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if greater than, unsigned vmsgtu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # Vector-scalar vmsgtu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if greater than, signed vmsgt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar vmsgt.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm    # Vector-immediate # Following two instructions are not provided directly # Set if greater than or equal, unsigned # vmsgeu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar # Set if greater than or equal, signed # vmsge.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar
```

The following table indicates how all comparisons are implemented in native machine code.

| Comparison                           | Assembler Mapping                                                                                           | Assembler Pseudoinstruction                           |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| va < vb va <= vb va > vb va >= vb    | vmslt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmslt{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm | vmsgt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsge{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm |
| va < x va <= x va > x va >= x va < i | vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsle{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm see below vm                  | vmslt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| va <= i va > i va >= i va, vb x      | vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vm    | vmsge{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| i                                    | vector register groups scalar integer register immediate                                                    |                                                       |

<image>

The  immediate  forms  of vmslt{u}.vi are  not  provided  as  the  immediate  value  can  be decreased by 1 and the vmsle{u}.vi variants used instead. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Because the 5-bit vector immediates are always sign-extended, when the high bit of the simm5 immediate is set, vmsleu.vi also supports unsigned immediate values in the range 2 SEW -16 to 2 SEW -1 ,  allowing  corresponding vmsltu.vi compares  against  unsigned  immediates  in  the range 2 SEW -15 to 2 SEW . Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```
unmasked va >= x pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x; vmnand.mm vd, vd, vd masked va >= x, vd != v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t; vmxor.mm vd, vd, v0 masked va >= x, vd == v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, vt masked va >= x, any vd pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vt, v0, vt;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, v0;  vmor.mm vd, vt, vd The vt argument to the pseudoinstruction must name a temporary vector register that is not same as vd and which will be clobbered by the pseudoinstruction
```

Compares effectively AND in the mask under a mask-undisturbed policy if the destination register is v0 , e.g.,

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask-undisturbed vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
```

Compares write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail-agnostic policy.

These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```
unmasked va >= x pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x; vmnand.mm vd, vd, vd masked va >= x, vd != v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t; vmxor.mm vd, vd, v0 masked va >= x, vd == v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, vt masked va >= x, any vd pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vt, v0, vt;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, v0;  vmor.mm vd, vt, vd The vt argument to the pseudoinstruction must name a temporary vector register that is not same as vd and which will be clobbered by the pseudoinstruction
```

Compares effectively AND in the mask under a mask-undisturbed policy if the destination register is v0 , e.g.,

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask-undisturbed vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
```

Compares write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail-agnostic policy.

The **vmsgtu.vx** instruction is a vector‑scalar integer compare that writes a mask value of 1 to each destination mask register element when the unsigned‑greater‑than comparison evaluates to true, and writes 0 otherwise.  
The destination mask vector is held in a single vector register; the register may be the same as the source vector mask register (**v0**).  

**Syntax**  
```
vmsgtu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # Vector‑scalar
```

**Assembler mapping** (from the comparison‑implementation table)

| Comparison | Assembler Mapping                                   |
|------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| va > x    | vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm                           |

Thus **vmsgtu.vx** implements the "unsigned greater‑than" compare for a vector register operand (**vs2**) and a scalar integer register operand (**rs1**).  

The vmsgt forms for register‑scalar and immediate operands are provided "to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions."  

All integer compare instructions, including **vmsgtu.vx**, "write mask registers, and so always operate under a *tail‑agnostic* policy."  

When the destination register is **v0**, compares "effectively **AND** in the mask under a *mask‑undisturbed* policy," e.g.:

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask‑undisturbed
vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written
vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
``` 

(The above example illustrates the generic mask‑undisturbed behavior, which also applies to **vmsgtu.vx**.)

## 31.3.4.3. Vector Tail Agnostic and Vector Mask Agnostic vta and vma

These  two  bits  modify  the  behavior  of  destination  tail  elements  and  destination  inactive  masked-off elements  respectively  during  the  execution  of  vector  instructions.  The  tail  and  inactive  sets  contain element positions that are not receiving new results during a vector operation, as defined in Section 31.5.4.

All systems must support all four options:

|   vta |   vma | Tail Elements   | Inactive Elements   |
|-------|-------|-----------------|---------------------|
|     0 |     0 | undisturbed     | undisturbed         |
|     0 |     1 | undisturbed     | agnostic            |
|     1 |     0 | agnostic        | undisturbed         |
|     1 |     1 | agnostic        | agnostic            |

Mask destination tail elements are always treated as tail-agnostic, regardless of the setting of vta .

When a set is marked undisturbed, the corresponding set of destination elements in a vector register group retain the value they previously held.

When a set is marked agnostic, the corresponding set of destination elements in any vector destination operand can either retain the value they previously held, or are overwritten with 1s. Within a single vector instruction,  each  destination  element  can  be  either  left  undisturbed  or  overwritten  with  1s,  in  any combination,  and  the  pattern  of  undisturbed  or  overwritten  with  1s  is  not  required  to  be  deterministic when the instruction is executed with the same inputs.

<image>

The agnostic policy was added to accommodate machines with vector register renaming. With an undisturbed policy, all elements would have to be read from the old physical destination vector register to be copied into the new physical destination vector register. This causes an inefficiency when these inactive or tail values are not required for subsequent calculations.

<image>

The value of all 1s instead of all 0s was chosen for the overwrite value to discourage software developers from depending on the value written.

<image>

<image>

<image>

A  simple  in-order  implementation  can  ignore  the  settings  and  simply  execute  all  vector instructions using the undisturbed policy. The vta and vma state bits must still be provided in vtype for compatibility and to support thread migration.

An out-of-order implementation can choose to implement tail-agnostic + mask-agnostic using tail-agnostic + mask-undisturbed to reduce implementation complexity.

The  definition  of  agnostic  result  policy  is  left  loose  to  accommodate  migrating  application threads  between  harts  on  a  small  in-order  core  (which  probably  leaves  agnostic  regions undisturbed) and harts on a larger out-of-order core with register renaming (which probably overwrites  agnostic  elements  with  1s).  As  it  might  be  necessary  to  restart  in  the  middle,  we allow  arbitrary  mixing  of  agnostic  policies  within  a  single  vector  instruction.  This  allowed mixing  of  policies  also  enables  implementations  that  might  change  policies  for  different granules of a vector register, for example, using undisturbed within a granule that is actively operated on but renaming to all 1s for granules in the tail.

In addition, except for mask load instructions, any element in the tail of a mask result can also be written with  the  value  the  mask-producing  operation  would  have  calculated  with vl =VLMAX. Furthermore, for mask-logical instructions and vmsbf.m , vmsif.m , vmsof.m mask-manipulation instructions, any element in the tail of the result can be written with the value the mask-producing operation would have calculated with vl =VLEN, SEW=8, and LMUL=8 (i.e., all bits of the mask register can be overwritten).

<image>

Mask tails are always treated as agnostic to reduce complexity of managing mask data, which can  be  written  at  bit  granularity.  There  appears  to  be  little  software  need  to  support  tailundisturbed for mask register values. Allowing mask-generating instructions to write back the result  of  the  instruction  avoids  the  need  for  logic  to  mask  out  the  tail,  except  mask  loads cannot write memory values to destination mask tails as this would imply accessing memory past software intent.

The assembly syntax adds two mandatory flags to the vsetvli instruction:

```
ta   # Tail agnostic tu   # Tail undisturbed ma   # Mask agnostic mu   # Mask undisturbed vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, ta, ma   # Tail agnostic, mask agnostic vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, tu, ma   # Tail undisturbed, mask agnostic vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, ta, mu   # Tail agnostic, mask undisturbed vsetvli t0, a0, e32, m4, tu, mu   # Tail undisturbed, mask undisturbed
```

<image>

Prior  to  v0.9,  when  these  flags  were  not  specified  on  a vsetvli ,  they  defaulted  to  maskundisturbed/tail-undisturbed. The use of vsetvli without these flags is deprecated, however, and  specifying  a  flag  setting  is  now  mandatory.  The  default  should  perhaps  be  tailagnostic/mask-agnostic, so software has to specify when it cares about the non-participating elements,  but  given  the  historical  meaning  of  the  instruction  prior  to  introduction  of  these flags, it was decided to always require them in future assembly code.
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- VMSIF.M is a mask‑manipulation instruction.  
- For mask‑manipulation instructions (including VMSIF.M), any element in the tail of the result **can be written** with the value the mask‑producing operation would have calculated with vl = VLEN, SEW = 8, and LMUL = 8 (i.e., all bits of the mask register can be overwritten).  
- Mask tails are always treated as **agnostic**; therefore the tail elements of a mask result may be left undisturbed or overwritten with 1s, and implementations are permitted to write any value permitted by the agnostic policy.

## 31.15.5. vmsif.m set-including-first mask bit

## 31.15.7. Example using vector mask instructions

The following is an example of vectorizing a data-dependent exit loop.

```
# char* strcpy(char *dst, const char* src) strcpy: mv a2, a0             # Copy dst li t0, -1             # Infinite AVL loop: vsetvli x0, t0, e8, m8, ta, ma  # Max length vectors of bytes vle8ff.v v8, (a1)        # Get src bytes csrr t1, vl           # Get number of bytes fetched
```

```
vmseq.vi v1, v8, 0      # Flag zero bytes vfirst.m a3, v1         # Zero found? add a1, a1, t1        # Bump pointer vmsif.m v0, v1          # Set mask up to and including zero byte. vse8.v v8, (a2), v0.t    # Write out bytes add a2, a2, t1        # Bump pointer bltz a3, loop         # Zero byte not found, so loop ret
```

```
# char* strncpy(char *dst, const char* src, size_t n) strncpy: mv a3, a0             # Copy dst loop: vsetvli x0, a2, e8, m8, ta, ma   # Vectors of bytes. vle8ff.v v8, (a1)        # Get src bytes vmseq.vi v1, v8, 0      # Flag zero bytes csrr t1, vl           # Get number of bytes fetched vfirst.m a4, v1         # Zero found? vmsbf.m v0, v1          # Set mask up to before zero byte. vse8.v v8, (a3), v0.t    # Write out non-zero bytes bgez a4, zero_tail    # Zero remaining bytes. sub a2, a2, t1        # Decrement count. add a3, a3, t1        # Bump dest pointer add a1, a1, t1        # Bump src pointer bnez a2, loop         # Anymore? ret zero_tail: sub a2, a2, a4          # Subtract count on non-zero bytes. add a3, a3, a4          # Advance past non-zero bytes. vsetvli t1, a2, e8, m8, ta, ma   # Vectors of bytes. vmv.v.i v0, 0           # Splat zero. zero_loop: vse8.v v0, (a3)          # Store zero. sub a2, a2, t1        # Decrement count. add a3, a3, t1        # Bump pointer vsetvli t1, a2, e8, m8, ta, ma   # Vectors of bytes. bnez a2, zero_loop    # Anymore? ret
```
============================================================
=========
RESPONSE:
=========
============================================================
- **Instruction form:** `vmsif.m v0, v1`  

- **Behavior (as described in the example):**  
  - The instruction **sets a mask up to and including the zero byte** that is flagged in the source mask `v1`.  

- **Context of use (from the example):**  
  - `v1` is produced by `vmseq.vi v1, v8, 0`, which flags zero bytes in a vector `v8`.  
  - `vmsif.m v0, v1` then creates a mask `v0` that is active for all elements **up to and including** the first element where `v1` is true (i.e., the first zero byte).  

No other explicit, normative architectural details about `vmsif.m` are provided in the given text.

## 31.11.8. Vector Integer Compare Instructions

The  following  integer  compare  instructions  write  1  to  the  destination  mask  register  element  if  the comparison  evaluates  to  true,  and  0  otherwise.  The  destination  mask  vector  is  always  held  in  a  single vector  register,  with  a  layout  of  elements  as  described  in  Section  31.4.5.  The  destination  mask  vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register ( v0 ).

```
# Set if equal vmseq.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmseq.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmseq.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if not equal vmsne.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsne.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsne.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if less than, unsigned vmsltu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsltu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # Vector-scalar # Set if less than, signed vmslt.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmslt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar # Set if less than or equal, unsigned vmsleu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm   # Vector-vector vmsleu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # vector-scalar vmsleu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if less than or equal, signed vmsle.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsle.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsle.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if greater than, unsigned vmsgtu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # Vector-scalar vmsgtu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if greater than, signed vmsgt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar vmsgt.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm    # Vector-immediate # Following two instructions are not provided directly # Set if greater than or equal, unsigned # vmsgeu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar # Set if greater than or equal, signed # vmsge.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar
```

The following table indicates how all comparisons are implemented in native machine code.

| Comparison                           | Assembler Mapping                                                                                           | Assembler Pseudoinstruction                           |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| va < vb va <= vb va > vb va >= vb    | vmslt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmslt{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm | vmsgt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsge{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm |
| va < x va <= x va > x va >= x va < i | vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsle{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm see below vm                  | vmslt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| va <= i va > i va >= i va, vb x      | vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vm    | vmsge{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| i                                    | vector register groups scalar integer register immediate                                                    |                                                       |

<image>

The  immediate  forms  of vmslt{u}.vi are  not  provided  as  the  immediate  value  can  be decreased by 1 and the vmsle{u}.vi variants used instead. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Because the 5-bit vector immediates are always sign-extended, when the high bit of the simm5 immediate is set, vmsleu.vi also supports unsigned immediate values in the range 2 SEW -16 to 2 SEW -1 ,  allowing  corresponding vmsltu.vi compares  against  unsigned  immediates  in  the range 2 SEW -15 to 2 SEW . Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```

- **Operation**: `vmsle.vi` is an integer compare instruction that *writes 1 to the destination mask‑register element if the signed "less‑than‑or‑equal" comparison evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise*.

- **Destination mask register**: The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5. The destination mask register may be the same as the source vector mask register (`v0`).

- **Immediate operand range**: The 5‑bit immediate field of `vmsle.vi` is sign‑extended; the immediate value **must be in the range ‑16 to 15**. (The effective range for the related `vmslt.vi` operation is ‑15 to 16, but `vmslt.vi` is not provided directly.)

- **Mask‑policy**: `vmsle.vi` writes mask registers and therefore *always operates under a tail‑agnostic policy*.

- **Shared behavior**: All integer compare instructions, including `vmsle.vi`, share the behavior described above (write 1/0 to the mask element, single‑register destination layout, possible use of `v0` as source mask, tail‑agnostic operation).

## 31.11.8. Vector Integer Compare Instructions

The  following  integer  compare  instructions  write  1  to  the  destination  mask  register  element  if  the comparison  evaluates  to  true,  and  0  otherwise.  The  destination  mask  vector  is  always  held  in  a  single vector  register,  with  a  layout  of  elements  as  described  in  Section  31.4.5. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

- **Operation**: For each element *i* of the source vectors, the instruction **writes 1 to the destination mask register element** `vd[i]` **if the signed integer comparison** `vs2[i] ≤ vs1[i]` **evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise**.  
  This behavior follows the general rule for the integer compare instructions: *"write 1 to the destination mask register element if the comparison evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise."*

- **Destination mask register**: The destination mask vector is **always held in a single vector register**, with the element layout defined in Section 31.4.5. The destination mask register **may be the same as the source vector mask register (`v0`)**.

- **Mask‑policy**: Because the instruction **writes mask registers**, it **always operates under a tail‑agnostic policy**.  
  If the destination register is `v0`, the instruction **effectively ANDs in the mask under a mask‑undisturbed policy** (the same policy described for other compare instructions, e.g., `vmslt.vv`).  

- **Assembler mapping**: In the comparison‑mapping table, the entry "`va <= vb`" is implemented as `vmsle{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm`. For the signed case the mapping is `vmsle.vv vd, va, vb, vm`.  

- **No additional encodings**: `vmsle.vv` is provided directly; there is no mention of it being synthesized from other instructions.  

- **No special exception or permission behavior** is specified for `vmsle.vv` beyond the general compare‑instruction behavior.

- **Operation**: `vmsle.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm` performs a signed "less‑than‑or‑equal" compare between each element of source vector register `vs2` and the scalar integer register `rs1`. For each element, the instruction writes **1** to the corresponding element of the destination mask register `vd` if the comparison evaluates to true, and **0** otherwise.

- **Mask handling**: The instruction writes mask registers, and therefore always operates under a **tail‑agnostic policy**. When the destination register is `v0`, the compare effectively ANDs the result into the mask under a **mask‑undisturbed policy** (i.e., only mask bits that are set remain set).  

- **Assembler mapping**: In the native encoding table, the signed "less‑than‑or‑equal" compare with a scalar operand is mapped to the assembler mnemonic `vmsle.vx vd, va, x, vm`, where `va` is the source vector, `x` is the scalar integer register, and `vm` is the optional mask.  

These points constitute the explicit, normative architectural behavior of the `VMSLE.VX` instruction as described in the source text.

<image>

The  immediate  forms  of vmslt{u}.vi are  not  provided  as  the  immediate  value  can  be decreased by 1 and the vmsle{u}.vi variants used instead. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Because the 5-bit vector immediates are always sign-extended, when the high bit of the simm5 immediate is set, vmsleu.vi also supports unsigned immediate values in the range 2 SEW -16 to 2 SEW -1 ,  allowing  corresponding vmsltu.vi compares  against  unsigned  immediates  in  the range 2 SEW -15 to 2 SEW . Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```
unmasked va >= x pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x; vmnand.mm vd, vd, vd masked va >= x, vd != v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t; vmxor.mm vd, vd, v0 masked va >= x, vd == v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, vt masked va >= x, any vd pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vt, v0, vt;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, v0;  vmor.mm vd, vt, vd The vt argument to the pseudoinstruction must name a temporary vector register that is not same as vd and which will be clobbered by the pseudoinstruction
```

Compares effectively AND in the mask under a mask-undisturbed policy if the destination register is v0 , e.g.,

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask-undisturbed vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
```

Compares write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail-agnostic policy.

- **Instruction form**: `vmsleu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm` # Vector‑immediate # Set if less than or equal, unsigned  

- **Result semantics**: The integer compare instructions write **1** to the destination mask register element if the comparison evaluates to true, and **0** otherwise. (Applies to `vmsleu.vi`.)

- **Destination mask register**:  
  * The destination mask vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register (`v0`).  
  * The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5.

- **Immediate‑value range**:  
  * The `vmsleu.vi` immediate range is **0 to 15**.  
  * This gives an effective `vmsltu.vi` range of **1 to 16** (note: `vmsltu.vi` with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

- **Sign‑extension behavior**: Because the 5‑bit vector immediates are always sign‑extended, when the high bit of the `simm5` immediate is set, `vmsleu.vi` also supports unsigned immediate values in the range **2 SEW − 16 to 2 SEW − 1**, allowing corresponding `vmsltu.vi` compares against unsigned immediates in the range **2 SEW − 15 to 2 SEW**. (Note: `vmsltu.vi` with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.)

- **Mask‑policy**: Comparisons write mask registers, and so always operate under a **tail‑agnostic** policy.  

- **Mask‑undisturbed behavior**: Comparisons effectively **AND** in the mask under a **mask‑undisturbed** policy if the destination register is `v0`.

- **Mnemonic and encoding**  
  `vmsleu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm`  Vector‑vector form of the *Set if less than or equal, unsigned* instruction.

- **Functional behavior**  
  The instruction "writes 1 to the destination mask register element if the comparison evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise."  For `vmsleu.vv` the comparison is **unsigned less‑or‑equal** between the corresponding elements of the source vectors `vs2` and `vs1`.  Thus each mask‑element in `vd` is set to 1 when `vs2[i] ≤_u vs1[i]`; otherwise it is set to 0.

- **Destination mask register**  
  The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5.  The destination mask register may be the same as the source mask register (register v0).

- **Tail‑agnostic policy**  
  Compare instructions write mask registers, and therefore **always operate under a tail‑agnostic policy**.

- **Mask‑undisturbed policy**  
  When the destination register is `v0`, the compare "effectively AND in the mask under a mask‑undisturbed policy."  In this case only the mask bits that are already set are updated; elements whose mask is clear remain unchanged.

- **Assembler mapping (implementation)**  

  | Comparison | Assembler mapping for unsigned ≤ |
  |------------|-----------------------------------|
  | `va ≤ vb`  | `vmsleu.vv vd, va, vb, vm`        |

**Syntax**  
`vmsleu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm`  # vector‑scalar (unsigned less‑than‑or‑equal)

**Functional behavior**  
The instruction writes **1** to each element of the destination mask register element if the unsigned comparison "*vs2 element* ≤ *scalar integer register rs1*" evaluates to true, and **0** otherwise.

**Destination mask register**  
- The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5.  
- The destination mask vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register (`v0`).

**Policy**  
- Compare instructions write mask registers, and therefore **always operate under a tail‑agnostic policy**.  
- When the destination register is `v0`, compare instructions **effectively AND in the mask under a mask‑undisturbed policy** (i.e., they preserve previously set mask bits).

**Assembler mapping**  
The "*va ≤ x*" comparison is implemented by the instruction:

| Comparison | Assembler mapping |
|------------|-------------------|
| `va ≤ x`   | `vmsle{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm` |

Thus, `vmsleu.vx` implements the unsigned "≤" comparison of each element of vector register `vs2` against the scalar integer register `rs1`, producing a mask in `vd` under the policies described above.

## 31.11.8. Vector Integer Compare Instructions

The  following  integer  compare  instructions  write  1  to  the  destination  mask  register  element  if  the comparison  evaluates  to  true,  and  0  otherwise.  The  destination  mask  vector  is  always  held  in  a  single vector  register,  with  a  layout  of  elements  as  described  in  Section  31.4.5.  The  destination  mask  vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register ( v0 ).

```
# Set if equal vmseq.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmseq.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmseq.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if not equal vmsne.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsne.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsne.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if less than, unsigned vmsltu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsltu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # Vector-scalar # Set if less than, signed vmslt.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmslt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar # Set if less than or equal, unsigned vmsleu.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm   # Vector-vector vmsleu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # vector-scalar vmsleu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if less than or equal, signed vmsle.vv vd, vs2, vs1, vm  # Vector-vector vmsle.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm  # vector-scalar vmsle.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm  # vector-immediate # Set if greater than, unsigned vmsgtu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm   # Vector-scalar vmsgtu.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm   # Vector-immediate # Set if greater than, signed vmsgt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar vmsgt.vi vd, vs2, imm, vm    # Vector-immediate # Following two instructions are not provided directly # Set if greater than or equal, unsigned # vmsgeu.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar # Set if greater than or equal, signed # vmsge.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm    # Vector-scalar
```

The following table indicates how all comparisons are implemented in native machine code.

| Comparison                           | Assembler Mapping                                                                                           | Assembler Pseudoinstruction                           |
|--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------|
| va < vb va <= vb va > vb va >= vb    | vmslt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmslt{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm vmsle{u}.vv vd, vb, va, vm | vmsgt{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm vmsge{u}.vv vd, va, vb, vm |
| va < x va <= x va > x va >= x va < i | vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsle{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, x, vm see below vm                  | vmslt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| va <= i va > i va >= i va, vb x      | vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vmsle{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm vmsgt{u}.vi vd, va, i-1, vm    | vmsge{u}.vi vd, va, i, vm                             |
| i                                    | vector register groups scalar integer register immediate                                                    |                                                       |

<image>

The  immediate  forms  of vmslt{u}.vi are  not  provided  as  the  immediate  value  can  be decreased by 1 and the vmsle{u}.vi variants used instead. The vmsle.vi range is -16 to 15, resulting in an effective vmslt.vi range of -15 to 16. The vmsleu.vi range is 0 to 15 giving an effective vmsltu.vi range of 1 to 16 (Note, vmsltu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always false).

<image>

Because the 5-bit vector immediates are always sign-extended, when the high bit of the simm5 immediate is set, vmsleu.vi also supports unsigned immediate values in the range 2 SEW -16 to 2 SEW -1 ,  allowing  corresponding vmsltu.vi compares  against  unsigned  immediates  in  the range 2 SEW -15 to 2 SEW . Note that vmsltu.vi with immediate 2 SEW is not useful as it is always true.

Similarly, vmsge{u}.vi is  not  provided  and  the  compare  is  implemented  using vmsgt{u}.vi with  the immediate  decremented  by  one.  The  resulting  effective vmsge.vi range  is  -15  to  16,  and  the  resulting effective vmsgeu.vi range is 1 to 16 (Note, vmsgeu.vi with immediate 0 is not useful as it is always true).

<image>

The vmsgt forms for register scalar and immediates are provided to allow a single compare instruction to provide the correct polarity of mask value without using additional mask logical instructions.

To reduce encoding space, the vmsge{u}.vx form is not directly provided, and so the va ≥ x case requires special treatment.

<image>

The vmsge{u}.vx could  potentially  be  encoded  in  a  non-orthogonal  way  under  the  unused OPIVI variant of vmslt{u} . These would be the only instructions in OPIVI that use a scalar x register however. Alternatively, a further two funct6 encodings could be used, but these would have a different operand format (writes to mask register) than others in the same group of 8 funct6  encodings.  The  current  PoR  is  to  omit  these  instructions  and  to  synthesize  where needed as described below.

The vmsge{u}.vx operation can be synthesized by reducing the value of x by 1 and using the vmsgt{u}.vx instruction, when it is known that this will not underflow the representation in x .

```
Sequences to synthesize vmsge{u}.vx instruction va >= x,  x > minimum addi t0, x, -1; vmsgt{u}.vx vd, va, t0, vm
```

The above sequence will usually be the most efficient implementation, but assembler pseudoinstructions can be provided for cases where the range of x is unknown.

```
unmasked va >= x pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x; vmnand.mm vd, vd, vd masked va >= x, vd != v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t; vmxor.mm vd, vd, v0 masked va >= x, vd == v0 pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, vt masked va >= x, any vd pseudoinstruction: vmsge{u}.vx vd, va, x, v0.t, vt expansion: vmslt{u}.vx vt, va, x;  vmandn.mm vt, v0, vt;  vmandn.mm vd, vd, v0;  vmor.mm vd, vt, vd The vt argument to the pseudoinstruction must name a temporary vector register that is not same as vd and which will be clobbered by the pseudoinstruction
```

Compares effectively AND in the mask under a mask-undisturbed policy if the destination register is v0 , e.g.,

```
# (a < b) && (b < c) in two instructions when mask-undisturbed vmslt.vv    v0, va, vb        # All body elements written vmslt.vv    v0, vb, vc, v0.t  # Only update at set mask
```

Compares write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail-agnostic policy.
============================================================

============================================================

- **Operation**:  
  *Set if less than, signed* – the `vmslt.vx` instruction performs a signed less‑than comparison between each element of the source vector register `vs2` and the scalar integer register `rs1`.  

- **Result writing**:  
  The integer compare instructions *write 1 to the destination mask register element if the comparison evaluates to true, and 0 otherwise*. The destination mask vector is always held in a single vector register, with a layout of elements as described in Section 31.4.5. The destination mask vector register may be the same as the source vector mask register (`v0`).  

- **Assembler mapping**:  
  `vmslt.vx vd, vs2, rs1, vm`  *vector‑scalar* – implements the signed less‑than comparison described above, writing the mask result to destination mask register `vd` under the optional mask `vm`.  

- **Policy**:  
  Compare instructions *write mask registers, and so always operate under a tail‑agnostic policy*.  

- **Mask‑undisturbed behavior**:  
  When the destination register is `v0`, compares *effectively AND in the mask under a mask‑undisturbed policy*.
